passages.happening:
About that time, King Herod reaches out to harm some of the church (verse 1). “He had James, the brother of John, put to death with the sword” (verse 2).

Seeing that this pleases the Jews, he arrests Peter too, during the Feast of Unleavened Bread (verse 3). He puts him in prison under a guard of four squads of four soldiers each, and means to bring him out to the people after the Passover (verse 4).

“So Peter was kept in prison, but the church was fervently praying to God for him” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
This King Herod is not the Herod of Jesus' birth, nor the Herod who killed John the Baptist. Historians call him Herod Agrippa I. He was a grandson of Herod the Great, and a friend of the emperors Caligula and Claudius. In AD 41 Claudius gave him Judea and Samaria, so for about three years Judea had its own king again instead of a Roman governor. He sought the favour of the people he ruled.

James is one of the first disciples, the brother of John, one of the three closest to Jesus. Luke tells his death in one sentence. He is the first of the Twelve to die for Jesus.

‘This pleased the Jews.’ Luke means the people in Jerusalem whose favour Herod was seeking, above all the leaders who had opposed the apostles from the start. He does not mean every Jew. James and Peter were Jews, and so was the church praying through the night. The note on Acts 2:22-28 explains how verses like this were later misused against Jewish people, and why this site rejects that reading.

The Feast of Unleavened Bread was the week that began with Passover, when Jerusalem was full of pilgrims. Herod would not hold a trial during the feast, so Peter waited in prison. Sixteen soldiers guarding one fisherman shows how much Herod wanted him kept. Perhaps he remembered that the apostles had walked out of prison once before (5:19).

‘Fervently’ means earnestly, with the whole self, straining toward God. The church had no soldiers and no influence with the king. It had prayer.
passages.ot:
James dies as his Lord said he would. When James and John asked for the seats of honour, Jesus said, “You will drink the cup that I drink” (Mark 10:39). James is the first of the Twelve to drink it.

The Old Testament is honest that faithful people are not always spared. The letter to the Hebrews, looking back over Israel's story, tells of some who were rescued and others who “were put to death by the sword” (Hebrews 11:37). And a psalm says, “Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of His saints” (Psalm 116:15).

The timing is Passover, the feast of Israel's rescue from Egypt. God told Moses, “I have come down to rescue them from the hand of the Egyptians” (Exodus 3:8). A first hearer would wait to see whether God would rescue again.
passages.hard:
Why was James killed and Peter freed?

The text gives no reason. Luke tells James's death in a single sentence and Peter's rescue in many, and he does not explain why God let one apostle die and brought the other out. He does not say that James had less faith, or that the church prayed less for him, or that God loved Peter more. He simply tells what happened. These notes will not invent a reason Luke does not give.

The wider New Testament helps us hold the two together without explaining them away. Jesus had told James he would drink his cup (Mark 10:39), and he did. Jesus told Peter that he too would one day die for him (John 21:18-19), and early Christian writers tell that he was later killed in Rome under the emperor Nero. Peter's rescue was not a promise that he would never suffer. It was a reprieve. Both men belonged to God in life and in death.

If you have prayed for someone to be rescued, from illness, from danger, from prison, from death, and the rescue did not come, this chapter does not say your prayer was too weak. The church surely prayed for James too. The three friends in Daniel said God was able to deliver them, “But even if He does not” (Daniel 3:18), they would still trust him. Grief and confusion at such a loss are not a lack of faith. If the weight of it is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a counsellor. If the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The church did not know whether Peter would live or die. It prayed anyway, all night. Ask whether you pray only when you are sure of the answer you want. And remember James, whose death takes one verse. A short story in the Bible is not a small life to God.

passages.happening:
On the night before his trial, Peter is sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains, with guards at the door (verse 6).

Suddenly an angel of the Lord appears and a light shines in the cell. He strikes Peter on the side to wake him. “Get up quickly,” he says, and the chains fall off his wrists (verse 7). “Get dressed and put on your sandals,” the angel says, and then, “Wrap your cloak around you and follow me” (verse 8).

Peter follows, not knowing that it is real. He thinks he is seeing a vision (verse 9). They pass the first and second guards and come to the iron gate leading to the city, which opens for them by itself. They walk the length of one street, and the angel leaves him (verse 10).

Then Peter comes to himself. “Now I know for sure that the Lord has sent His angel and rescued me from Herod’s grasp and from everything the Jewish people were anticipating” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
The night before a trial that would likely end in his death, Peter is asleep. Chained between two soldiers, he sleeps. That is a picture of peace. Perhaps he remembered Jesus' words that he would grow old (John 21:18).

The angel has to strike him to wake him, and then tell him each step like a parent with a sleepy child: get up, get dressed, put on your sandals, wrap your cloak around you. Luke tells it with a smile. Even after the iron gate swings open by itself, Peter thinks he is dreaming. Only out in the cold street does he understand.

‘Everything the Jewish people were anticipating’ means the crowd in Jerusalem that Herod meant to please, waiting for the trial after the feast. Again, it does not mean all Jews: the people praying for Peter that night were Jews too.
passages.ot:
The story is full of Passover. On the first Passover night God kept watch over Israel: “the LORD kept a vigil that night to bring them out of the land of Egypt” (Exodus 12:42). Israel ate that meal “fully dressed for travel, with your sandals on your feet” (Exodus 12:11). Now, at Passover again, an angel tells Peter to get dressed, put on his sandals, and walk out.

Peter's words, ‘the Lord has sent His angel and rescued me’, echo the Psalms: “The angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear Him, and he delivers them” (Psalm 34:7). And a psalm of return from exile says, “When the LORD restored the captives of Zion, we were like dreamers” (Psalm 126:1). Peter, too, thought he was dreaming.
passages.asks: Peter slept in chains on the night before his trial. Ask what gives you peace when you cannot change what tomorrow holds. And notice that the rescue came step by step: get up, dress, follow. Often God leads one step at a time, and understanding comes after obedience.

passages.happening:
Peter goes to the house of Mary, the mother of John, also called Mark, where many people have gathered to pray (verse 12). He knocks at the outer gate, and a servant girl named Rhoda comes to answer (verse 13). She knows his voice, and she is so overjoyed that she forgets to open the gate. She runs in and announces, “Peter is standing at the gate!” (verse 14).

“You are out of your mind,” they tell her. When she keeps insisting, they say, “It must be his angel” (verse 15). But Peter keeps on knocking. When they open the door and see him, they are astounded (verse 16).

Peter motions for silence and tells how the Lord brought him out of prison. “Send word to James and to the brothers,” he says, and he leaves for another place (verse 17).

At daybreak there is great alarm among the soldiers. Herod searches for Peter without success, questions the guards, and orders them executed. Then he goes down from Judea to Caesarea (verses 18-19).
passages.hearers:
This is one of the most human scenes in the Bible. The church has prayed all night for Peter's release. Then Peter is at the gate, and they tell the girl who says so that she is mad.

Rhoda's name means ‘rose’. She is a servant girl, perhaps a slave, the least important person in the house. Yet she is the first to know, and the first to announce the good news, while the praying leaders do not believe her. Luke may want his readers to remember the women at the empty tomb, whose news the apostles thought was nonsense (Luke 24:11).

‘It must be his angel’ reflects a belief of the time that each person had an angel, who might even look or sound like him. Jesus spoke of children's ‘angels in heaven’ (Matthew 18:10).

Mary's house had an outer gate, a servant, and room for many people, so she was likely a woman of some means. The early church had no buildings; it met in homes like this. Her son John Mark will travel with Barnabas and Saul (12:25). Early Christian writers linked a Mark with the Gospel that bears his name.

‘Send word to James’: this James is not the apostle who was just killed. He is James the brother of Jesus, who becomes a leader of the church in Jerusalem (15:13; Galatians 1:19).

The guards' fate is grim. Luke does not explain it, but many think guards were held responsible for a prisoner they lost; in Philippi a jailer who thought his prisoners had escaped was ready to kill himself (16:27). Herod's cruelty to his own men is part of his portrait.
passages.ot:
The house full of people who cannot believe their prayers have been answered has an echo in the Psalms: “When the LORD restored the captives of Zion, we were like dreamers” (Psalm 126:1). Joy can feel too good to be true.

Peter leaves ‘for another place’. Like the prophets in danger, he hides. Elijah fled from Jezebel (1 Kings 19:3), and the faithful hid the prophets in caves (1 Kings 18:4). Escape is not a failure of faith.
passages.asks: The church prayed for Peter's release, and then could not believe it when he knocked. Ask whether you pray without expecting God to answer. And honour Rhoda. The least important person in the room was the first to believe the good news, and she would not stop saying it.

passages.happening:
Herod is in a furious dispute with the people of Tyre and Sidon. They win over Blastus, the king's chamberlain, and ask for peace, because their region depends on the king's country for food (verse 20).

On the appointed day, Herod puts on his royal robes, sits on his throne, and speaks to the people. They begin to shout, “This is the voice of a god, not a man!” (verse 22). “Immediately, because Herod did not give glory to God, an angel of the Lord struck him down, and he was eaten by worms and died” (verse 23).

“But the word of God continued to spread and multiply” (verse 24). Barnabas and Saul, their task in Jerusalem done, return to Antioch, bringing John, also called Mark (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
Tyre and Sidon were old port cities on the coast north of Galilee. Luke says their region depended on the lands Herod ruled for food. A quarrel with him threatened their food. A chamberlain was a trusted officer of the king's household, and they won him over to plead for them.

The Jewish historian Josephus tells of Herod Agrippa's death too. As he tells it, the king came to games at Caesarea held in honour of the emperor, wearing a robe made all of silver that shone in the morning sun. Flatterers called him a god, and he did not stop them. Soon after he was seized with terrible pain in his belly, and he died five days later. Josephus places it in the seventh year of Claudius, AD 44. The two accounts differ in detail, but they agree on the place, the crowd's cry, the king's silence, and the sudden, painful death. Because this death can be dated, it is one of the few fixed points for the timeline of Acts.

Luke gives the reason in one plain phrase: ‘because Herod did not give glory to God’. He took for himself the worship that belongs to God alone.

Then the turn: ‘But the word of God continued to spread.’ The chapter began with Herod reaching out his hand against the church. It ends with Herod dead and the word growing.
passages.ot:
The Old Testament knows proud kings who think themselves gods. Of the ruler of Tyre, God said through Ezekiel, “you have said, ‘I am a god; I sit in the seat of gods in the heart of the sea.’ Yet you are a man and not a god” (Ezekiel 28:2). King Nebuchadnezzar boasted of “the glory of my majesty” (Daniel 4:30), and was humbled until he praised “the King of heaven”, who “is able to humble those who walk in pride” (Daniel 4:37).

God says through Isaiah, “I will not yield My glory to another or My praise to idols” (Isaiah 42:8). Herod accepted praise as a god, and the angel who had freed Peter struck down the king.

Tyre's dependence on Israel's food is old too. Long before, King Hiram of Tyre sent timber to Solomon, and “year after year Solomon would provide Hiram with 20,000 cors of wheat as food for his household” (1 Kings 5:11).
passages.asks: Herod wanted to be admired. The crowd gave him what he wanted, and it was the end of him. Ask where you are tempted to take praise that belongs to God: for your gifts, your success, your goodness. And take heart from verse 24. Rulers rise and fall. ‘The word of God continued to spread.’
